what_it_does: Modern edge devices — like a smartphone's system-on-chip — contain several different kinds of computing units: a general-purpose CPU, a GPU (graphics processor repurposed for AI math), an NPU (a neural-network accelerator), and sometimes a TPU (a tensor/matrix-math accelerator). Existing software frameworks treat each unit independently and do not know which part of the AI model is the bottleneck slowing everything else down. InfScaler first profiles the model to identify that bottleneck, then applies 'asymmetric auto-scaling': it deliberately allocates more compute resources to the slow stage and fewer to the fast ones — unlike symmetric approaches that split resources evenly — so the pipeline flows without one stage perpetually waiting. Because these edge chips share a single pool of memory accessible by all units (unified memory), data can be handed off between asymmetrically assigned partitions without expensive copying.
